name: Stiletto beard

card.summary: A narrow, sharply pointed chin beard that lengthens the chin and draws the eye down the centre of the face.
card.note: Name and exact shape vary by source; the term is historical and used loosely in grooming.

quick.overview:
The stiletto beard is a facial-hair style in which the beard is kept narrow and trimmed to a sharp point at the chin, named for the slim stiletto dagger. Wearers use pointed chin beards to add apparent length to the chin and to frame the lower face with a defined vertical line.

The style belongs to the family of pointed chin beards that includes the goatee and the Van Dyke. Wikipedia lists the stiletto among 16th-century European beard styles, alongside the Spanish spade, English square cut and forked beard; no studies have examined it specifically.
quick.how: In practice it is a grooming choice: the beard is grown on the chin and shaped with trimmers and a razor so that the sides are narrow and the lower end tapers. Cheeks are typically kept clean or closely trimmed, and the point is maintained with regular touch-ups.
quick.risks: Facial hair styling is low-risk beyond ordinary razor irritation or ingrown hairs. The look depends on beard growth pattern, and sparse chin growth can limit what shape is achievable.

lead: The stiletto beard is a narrow, pointed chin beard. Wikipedia's article on beards names it among the beards of 16th-century Europe, alongside the Spanish spade, the English square cut and the forked beard, but does not describe its shape [1]. The name evokes the stiletto, a thin dagger, and in grooming usage points to a slender, tapering chin beard.

How it helps looks is a matter of shape. A pointed chin beard lengthens the chin vertically and can make a round or wide lower face look longer, while the narrow width leaves the cheeks and jawline sides bare. Wikipedia notes in a general discussion that beards may signal dominance by increasing perceived jaw size, and that clean-shaven faces are rated less dominant than bearded ones [1].

It sits within a long history of pointed chin beards. Beards became more trimmed and pointed at the start of the 17th century, and men around the mid-17th century commonly wore a mustache or pointed goatee [1]. The Van Dyke, a goatee-plus-mustache style named after painter Anthony van Dyck, grew popular in Europe in that century and again in the US in the 19th [2].

chain: Grow chin hair and trim it narrow to a point
Chin appears longer and the lower face centre is emphasised
Different face-shape balance and a defined, styled look
angle.text: Shaping the beard into a narrow point adds vertical length at the chin and frames the lower face with a defined line.

paras: The stiletto is named in historical lists of European beard styles from the 16th century, when beards were common among monarchs and nobles, especially after the Reformation [1]. Surviving descriptions are sparse, but the name implies a slender, tapered shape.

Related styles are better documented. A goatee is chin hair, and since the 1990s the word has been an umbrella term for chin styles that leave the cheeks bare [3]. The Van Dyke combines a goatee and mustache with shaved cheeks [2].

Pointed beards narrowed further in the early 17th century and fell out of fashion in the late 17th and 18th centuries, returning in the 19th [1]. The goatee itself traces to ancient Greece and Rome, and returned in the 1950s with beatniks in the United States [3].
No studies found. Research on beards generally, such as ratings of dominance for bearded versus clean-shaven faces, is a broader category that does not address this style [1].

timeline.event: The stiletto beard is listed among European beard fashions with the Spanish spade, English square cut and forked beard [1].
Beards grow narrower and more pointed; the Van Dyke becomes popular [1][2].
Goatees and Van Dykes become common US styles [1].
